analogy.p: Imagine two people holding opposite ends of a rope. If you pull on your partner, you can feel them pulling on you with exactly the same strength: you cannot pull without being pulled. That is the third law: the pull on them and the pull on you are equal and opposite, and each acts on a different person. It breaks down because in a real tug-of-war the winner is decided by friction with the ground and the resultant force on each team, not by the rope forces, which are always equal.
analogy.t: Two people on a tug-of-war rope

bullets: Forces always come in **pairs**, called **interaction pairs** (or action-reaction pairs).
The two forces in a pair are **equal in size** (magnitude) and **opposite in direction**.
They act on **different objects**: one on A, one on B. This is the key idea examiners test.
They are the **same type of force** (both contact, both gravitational, both magnetic, and so on).
The law applies to **contact forces** (pushes, friction, tension) and **non-contact forces** (gravity, magnetism, electrostatic force).
It holds at every instant, even when the objects are accelerating or colliding.
A common wording in mark schemes: **'the forces are equal and opposite and act on different objects'**.
core.p: **Newton's third law** says that **whenever two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite**. Forces never come singly: a force is always one half of an interaction between two objects. If object A pushes or pulls on object B, then object B must push or pull on object A with a force of exactly the same size, along the same line, in the opposite direction. This is true whether the objects touch or not, whether they are moving or still, and whether they are heavy or light.

bullets: Pair rule: **force of A on B** is paired with **force of B on A**.
Both forces have the **same size**, **opposite direction** and act along the **same line**.
They are the **same type**: contact with contact, gravitational with gravitational.
They act on **different objects**, so they can never be added together to find a resultant force on one object.
To check a pair, write both as sentences: 'X pushes Y' and 'Y pushes X'.
If both forces in your 'pair' act on the same object, they are not an interaction pair.
If the two forces are different types (for example weight and a contact force), they are not an interaction pair.
core.h: What counts as an interaction pair
core.p: To identify a pair, ask: 'What is the object that is exerting this force, and what is it acting on?' The partner force is then found by swapping the two objects around. If the force is 'the table pushes up on the book', the partner is 'the book pushes down on the table'. The partner always has the same wording with the two objects swapped, which is the safest way to check you have the right force.

bullets: **Pair 1 (gravity):** Earth pulls book down (the book's **weight**) and book pulls Earth up. Both are gravitational forces.
**Pair 2 (contact):** table pushes book up (the **normal contact force**) and book pushes table down. Both are contact forces.
The two forces on the book (weight down, contact force up) are equal and opposite only because the book is in **equilibrium**, not because of the third law.
If the table were removed, the book's weight would still be there but the contact force would vanish, proving they are not an interaction pair.
Each force on the book has its partner on a **different object** (the Earth or the table).
A free-body diagram of the book shows only the two forces **acting on the book**.
core.h: Worked example of pairs: a book on a table
core.p: A book at rest on a table has two forces acting on it, and each belongs to a different interaction pair. The weight of the book is the pull of the Earth on the book, so its partner is the pull of the book on the Earth (upward, acting on the Earth). The upward contact force from the table on the book is paired with the downward push of the book on the table. Identifying both pairs shows why the book stays still and why the pairs are not the same thing as balanced forces.

bullets: Weight and the contact force act on **one object** (the book); a third law pair acts on **two objects**.
They are **different types** of force.
Their equality depends on the situation: in a lift accelerating upwards, the floor pushes up with **more** than your weight.
Third law pairs are **always** equal, no matter how the objects move.
In an exam, name the objects: 'the Earth pulls on the book and the book pulls on the Earth'.
Safer phrase for equilibrium: 'the forces are balanced so the resultant force is zero'.
core.h: Why weight and the normal reaction are not a pair
core.p: Students very often say 'the weight of the book and the reaction force of the table are an action-reaction pair'. This is wrong. They act on the same object (the book), and they are different types of force (gravitational and contact). They are equal and opposite only because the resultant force on the book is zero, which is explained by Newton's first law, not the third. If the table accelerated upwards, the contact force would be greater than the weight and the two would no longer be equal, yet the third law pairs would still be exactly equal.

bullets: Forces in a pair act on **different** objects, so they **cannot cancel** each other.
Acceleration of each object: **a = F / m**, using the force acting on that object.
Same force, smaller mass gives **larger acceleration**.
Two skaters push apart with 120 N: a 60 kg skater gets 120 / 60 = 2.0 m/s2, a 40 kg skater gets 120 / 40 = 3.0 m/s2, in opposite directions.
A tiny object colliding with a huge one feels the same force but changes its motion far more.
The Earth feels the same size force as a falling apple, but its acceleration is far too small to notice.
Link: the **second law** gives the motion, the **third law** gives the pair of forces.
core.p: A common puzzle is: 'if the forces are equal and opposite, why does anything ever move?' The answer is that the two forces of a pair act on **different objects**, so they never cancel. Each object has its own resultant force. Using **resultant force = mass x acceleration (F = m a)**, the acceleration of each object depends on its own mass. So when two objects push on each other with equal forces, the lighter one accelerates more. The third law tells you the forces; the second law tells you what each force does to its object.

bullets: **Walking:** foot pushes ground backwards; ground pushes foot (and you) forwards (friction).
**Swimming:** swimmer pushes water backwards; water pushes swimmer forwards.
**Jumping from a small boat:** you push the boat backwards, the boat pushes you forwards, so the boat moves away from the shore.
**Hitting a wall:** your hand pushes on the wall and the wall pushes back on your hand, with equal force; this is why it hurts.
**Rowing, car tyres, a ball bouncing:** each involves a push on a surface and an equal and opposite push back.
If there were no friction (ice), your foot could not push the ground back effectively and you could not walk.
The force that accelerates you is the one acting **on you**, not the one you exert.
core.p: Many familiar actions are the third law at work. In each case you push on something and it pushes back on you. Walking depends on friction: your foot pushes backwards on the ground, and the ground pushes forwards on your foot, and it is the forward force on you that accelerates you. Swimming works in the same way, with hands and feet pushing water backwards so the water pushes you forwards. Always describe both forces, say what each acts on, and say which one moves the object in the question.

bullets: Rocket pushes gas **backwards**; gas pushes rocket **forwards** (equal and opposite).
The forces act on **different objects** (gas and rocket), so the rocket can accelerate.
Rockets and jet engines work in the same way; propellers push air backwards.
Rockets work in **space** because the gas is the thing being pushed, not the air.
Balloon: air pushed out of the neck pushes the balloon the other way.
A fire hose pushes water forwards and the water pushes the hose back, which is why firefighters need to brace themselves.
Link to **momentum** (physics only): the rocket gains forward momentum equal to the backward momentum of the gas.
core.p: A rocket moves because it pushes hot gases out of its engine at high speed. The rocket exerts a force on the gas, pushing it backwards (downwards), and the gas exerts an equal and opposite force on the rocket, pushing it forwards (upwards). The rocket does not need to push against the ground or air: it only needs something to push on, and the exhaust gas provides that. This is why rockets work in the vacuum of space where there is no air at all.

bullets: **Gravity:** Earth pulls on you; you pull on Earth with an equal force (towards you, upwards).
**Earth and Moon:** each pulls on the other with an equal and opposite gravitational force.
**Magnets:** if magnet A pulls magnet B, B pulls A with the same size force, even if one magnet is much stronger.
**Electrostatics:** two charged objects exert equal and opposite forces on each other.
A small magnet and a large steel nail pull on each other equally; the lighter one accelerates more.
The forces are the same size but the **effects** (accelerations) depend on the mass of each object.
Weight is the force of the **Earth on you**; the partner is your pull on the Earth.
core.h: Non-contact pairs: gravity, magnets and charges
core.p: The third law is not just about pushes and pulls where objects touch. It applies to all forces. The Earth attracts the Moon, and the Moon attracts the Earth with an equal and opposite gravitational force. Two magnets attract or repel each other with equal and opposite forces, and so do two charged objects. These forces act over a distance, but the rule is the same: equal size, opposite direction, different objects, same type.

bullets: During a collision the forces on both objects rise to a maximum together and fall to zero together.
**Equal force** on a car and a lorry does not mean **equal damage**: a = F / m is much larger for the car.
The collision time is the same for both objects since they are in contact together.
Because force and time are equal, the **change in momentum** of each is equal and opposite (physics only), so total momentum is conserved.
Seat belts, air bags and crumple zones increase the time of impact, reducing the force on the person.
If two identical trolleys collide with equal and opposite velocities, they exert equal forces and have equal accelerations.
In data questions, check whether the forces shown are equal in size and opposite in direction.
core.p: In a collision, two objects exert forces on each other for a short time. The force on one object is always equal and opposite to the force on the other, at every instant. This means a plot of force against time for each object would be mirror images, with the same peak size. It does not matter whether one object is a lorry and the other a small car: the forces on each are equal in size, but the car, with less mass, has a much greater acceleration and so suffers more damage.

bullets: **Free-body diagram:** forces on one object only; the partner forces are on other objects and are left out.
Resultant force is found by adding forces on **one object**, never both members of a pair.
First law: no resultant force means constant velocity (including zero).
Second law: **F = m a**, applied to each object separately.
Third law pairs make **conservation of momentum** work: equal and opposite forces for the same time give equal and opposite changes in momentum (physics only).
Higher tier thinking: use the third law to deduce a missing force in a problem, then F = m a to find an acceleration.
Check: if a question asks for the 'reaction' to a force, identify the two objects first.
core.h: Link to other forces topics: free-body diagrams and momentum
core.p: Newton's three laws form a set. The **first law** says an object keeps its velocity (stays still or moves at constant speed in a straight line) unless a resultant force acts. The **second law** links resultant force to acceleration. The **third law** says that forces come in pairs between two objects. In a free-body diagram you draw only the forces acting on the one object you are studying, so you never draw both members of a third law pair on the same diagram. This keeps the idea of resultant force clear.

bullets: Always write: **'force of A on B'** and **'force of B on A'**.
Say **equal in size, opposite in direction**, and that they are the **same type of force**.
Explain acceleration with **resultant force and mass**, not the third law alone.
For 'explain why the forces do not cancel', answer: **they act on different objects**.
Use sketches with labelled arrows if allowed; label which object each force acts on.
In 6-mark questions, link the third law to a real example, a free-body diagram and F = m a.
core.h: Answering third law questions in exams
core.p: Examiners nearly always reward a structured answer: name both objects, state the forces are equal and opposite, and state that they act on different objects. For example, for 'a person pushes a wall', a full-mark answer is 'the person pushes on the wall with a force; the wall pushes on the person with an equal force in the opposite direction'. When asked why something accelerates, bring in the second law and the resultant force on that object. Avoid the word 'reaction' alone, since it is ambiguous.

bullets: Ratio rule: **a1 / a2 = m2 / m1** for two objects pushing on each other with equal force for the same time.
Find the force from one object's mass and acceleration, then use it for the other object.
Direction: the two accelerations are in **opposite directions**.
Units: force in newtons (N), mass in kilograms (kg), acceleration in m/s2.
Check answers: the larger acceleration must belong to the smaller mass.
Example: A (60 kg) accelerates at 2.0 m/s2, so F = 60 x 2.0 = 120 N; B (40 kg) has a = 120 / 40 = 3.0 m/s2.
core.h: Higher tier extension: deducing and calculating with pairs
core.p: At Higher tier you may have to combine the third law with F = m a. If two objects of known masses exert a force on each other, you can use the force acting on one to find the acceleration of the other. Because the forces are equal, the ratio of accelerations is the inverse of the ratio of masses. This is a quick check on any collision or push-off calculation: the object with half the mass must have twice the acceleration.

exam: 1 mark: state the law. Write 'when two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite'.
1 mark: name the second force in a pair by swapping the objects, for example 'the book pushes down on the table'.
2 marks: 'identify the pair' needs both forces named (with objects), and either equal size or opposite direction.
Key phrase to learn: 'the forces act on different objects, so they do not cancel out'.
For 'why does the weight not form an interaction pair with the contact force' say: same object, different types of force.
3 marks 'explain how a rocket moves': rocket pushes gas backwards; gas pushes rocket forwards with an equal and opposite force; so the rocket accelerates forwards.
Calculation questions: find the force on one object using F = m a, state that the other object feels the same force in the opposite direction, then find its acceleration with a = F / m.
4 marks: link the third law to F = m a to explain why a small object accelerates more than a large object when they push on each other.
6 mark questions: use a clear structure of identify objects, state equal and opposite forces, link to second law, give a conclusion; use bold terms and a labelled diagram.
Command words: 'state' needs a short fact; 'explain' needs a reason (because...); 'calculate' needs working with units; 'describe' needs the steps in order.
Always give direction in your answer when asked about a force: 'upwards', 'to the left', 'opposite to the force of A on B'.

mistakes.r: They act on the same object and are different types of force; the pair of weight is the book's pull on the Earth.
mistakes.w: Weight and the reaction force of the table are a third law pair.

mistakes.r: The two forces act on different objects, so they cannot cancel; each object has its own resultant force.
mistakes.w: The forces cancel out, so nothing can ever move.

mistakes.r: The forces are always equal in size; the smaller object just has a larger acceleration (a = F / m).
mistakes.w: The bigger object exerts a bigger force.

mistakes.r: State both forces with objects named: 'A pushes B' and 'B pushes A with an equal force in the opposite direction'.
mistakes.w: Using 'action' and 'reaction' without naming the objects.

mistakes.r: The rocket pushes the exhaust gas backwards and the gas pushes the rocket forwards; no air needed.
mistakes.w: A rocket needs air to push against.

mistakes.r: Your foot pushes backwards on the ground and the ground exerts an equal and opposite force on your foot, which moves you forwards.
mistakes.w: The ground does not push on you when you walk.

mistakes.r: They are equal and opposite at all times, whether objects accelerate or not.
mistakes.w: Third law forces are equal only when objects are at rest.

mistakes.r: A free-body diagram shows only forces acting on the one object being considered.
mistakes.w: Drawing both forces of a pair on one free-body diagram.

summary: You must know that whenever two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite, and be able to identify interaction pairs and apply the law to everyday and non-contact situations. It matters because it explains how walking, rockets and collisions work, and it is often confused with balanced forces in exams.

terms.d: Whenever two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite.
Two forces of the same type, equal in size and opposite in direction, acting on two different objects that are interacting.
A push or pull that acts on an object due to the interaction with another object; a vector quantity measured in newtons (N).
A single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object.
A force that acts between objects that are touching, for example friction, tension and normal contact force.
A force that acts between objects that are not touching, for example gravity, magnetic force and electrostatic force.
The force acting on an object due to gravity; the gravitational pull of the Earth on the object, equal to mass x gravitational field strength.
The force a surface exerts on an object resting on it, acting at right angles to the surface.
The state in which the resultant force on an object is zero, so forces are balanced.
A diagram showing all the forces acting on a single object, drawn as labelled arrows.
A quantity that has both magnitude and direction, such as force.
The acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass: F = m a.
If the resultant force on a stationary object is zero, the object remains stationary; if it is moving, it continues at the same speed and direction.
A property of moving objects equal to mass x velocity, measured in kg m/s (physics only).

worked.ans: The wall pushes on the student with a force of 80 N in the opposite direction (back towards the student); it is a contact force.
worked.q: A student pushes a wall with a force of 80 N. State the size and direction of the force the wall exerts on the student, and name the type of force. [3 marks]
steps: The student exerts 80 N on the wall, so the wall exerts a force on the student.
By Newton's third law the forces are equal in size and opposite in direction.

worked.ans: A: 2.0 m/s2 and B: 3.0 m/s2, in opposite directions.
worked.q: Two skaters push apart. Skater A has mass 60 kg and skater B has mass 40 kg. The force of A on B is 120 N. Calculate the acceleration of each skater. [4 marks]
steps: By the third law, the force of B on A is also 120 N in the opposite direction.
Use a = F / m for A: a = 120 / 60 = 2.0 m/s2.
Use a = F / m for B: a = 120 / 40 = 3.0 m/s2.
The accelerations are in opposite directions.

worked.ans: The apple pulls the Earth upwards with a force of 0.98 N; the Earth's acceleration is about 1.6 x 10^-25 m/s2, which is negligible because of its enormous mass.
worked.q: A 0.10 kg apple falls and its weight is 0.98 N (g = 9.8 N/kg). Describe the force on the Earth and explain why the Earth does not appear to accelerate. The Earth's mass is 6.0 x 10^24 kg. [4 marks]
steps: Weight is the pull of the Earth on the apple, so the apple pulls on the Earth with an equal force.
The force on the Earth is 0.98 N upwards (towards the apple).
This acceleration is far too small to notice because the Earth's mass is huge.
